### INTRODUCTION

Jitter on analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog converter sampling clocks presents a limit to the maximum signal-to-noise ratio that can be achieved (see Integrated Analog-to-Digital and Digital-to-Analog Converters by van de Plassche in the References section)In this application note, phase noise and jitter are defined

The power spectral density of phase noise and jitter is developed, time domain and frequency domain measurement techniques are described, limitations of laboratory equipment are explained, and correction factors to these techniques are provided

The theory presented is supported with experimental results applied to a real world problem.

### GENERAL DESCRIPTION


There are numerous techniques for generating clocks used in electronic equipment. Circuits include R-C feedback circuits, timers, oscillators, and crystals and crystal oscillators. Depending on circuit requirements, less expensive sources with higher phase noise (jitter) may be acceptable. However, recent devices demand better clock performance and, consequently, more costly clock sources. Similar demands are placed on the spectral purity of signals sampled by converters, especially frequency synthesizers used as sources in the testing of current higher performance converters. In the following section, definitions of phase noise and jitter are presented. Then a mathematical derivation is developed relating phase noise and jitter to their frequency representation. The frequency domain representations, or power spectral densities, are shown to directly provide a measure of phase noise/jitter

The theory developed is associated with analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog converters. A spectrum analyzer and an oscilloscope are used to measure a variety of signals. Finally, theory is coupled with experimental results applied to an AD9235 analog-to-digital converter (ADC).

Power spectral density (PSD) is a measure of the distribution of power within a system. It relates to the frequency content in a signal, and is used to analyze system performance. In signal processing, the power spectral density is a useful concept in understanding how energy is distributed across the frequency domain. For example, it can be used to measure the power of a signal at different frequencies, to detect peaks, and to determine the bandwidth of a signal.

The formula for power spectral density is
$$

  PSD \, (\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} S(f) \, e^{-j2 \pi f \omega} \, df

$$

where $S(f)$ is the power spectral density function, $e^{-j2 \pi f \omega}/\pi$ is the normalized power spectrum, and $df$ is the frequency resolution. The power spectral density is typically expressed as a dB, which is a relative measure of power that is scaled using a 10log.

In the context of multimedia, the power spectral density is often calculated by dividing the power of a signal across the frequency spectrum by a reference frequency. This reference frequency is typically set so that the signal energy has an average value of one. The power spectral density is also sometimes normalized to have a unit of dB, and is sometimes reported in units of power spectral density per hertz (Hz).

In audio and music applications, power spectral density is often plotted as a graph that represents the power of sound across the frequency spectrum. This graph is often known as a power spectrum. The x-axis of the graph represents the frequency, and the y-axis represents the power of sound (in dB relative to the reference frequency).

The power spectral density is an important tool for analyzing the characteristics of musical sounds. It can be used to identify specific frequencies that contribute to the overall volume of a sound, to detect harmonics and other characteristics of sound, and to compare the sound properties of different musical instruments.

The following formula relates the power spectral density of a sinusoidal signal to the power spectral density of the signal itself:

$$

  PSD \, (\omega) = \frac{1}{2} (J_1(\omega) + J_{-1}(\omega))
$$

where $J_k(\omega)$ are the Bessel functions of order $k$.

The power spectral density can be related to the power spectral density of the input signal using the convolution theorem. If the power spectral density of the signal is $S_1(\omega)$, and the power spectral density of the vector $f(t)$ is $S_2(\omega)$, then the power spectral density of the output is

$$

  PSD \, (\omega) = S_2(\omega) * S_1(\omega)
$$

where $*$ represents the convolution operator.

This formula can be used to predict the response of a system to an input signal. The more closely the system meets the conditions specified in the formula, the faster and more stable the response will be.

The power spectral density is also useful in designing hearing aids. Many hearing aids are designed to amplify certain frequencies in the input signal, but filters are designed to attenuate all the power other than the desired frequency. The power spectral density of the input signal is used to determine the amount of attenuation to be applied by the hearing aid.

The power spectral density can also be used to test the performance of audio systems. For example, a test audio signal is passed through an audio system to measure the power spectral density at various frequencies. The power spectral density is then analyzed to determine how well the system performs at different frequencies.

Overall, the power spectral density is a powerful tool for the analysis and design of audio systems. It can be used to analyze the performance of audio systems, to test these systems under various conditions, and to predict the response of a system to an input signal.

Please note that the formula described above is an approximate formula, and is only an approximation; more accurate approximations exist but are not easy to derive in a useful manner.

The magnitude is obtained with an envelope detector and is given by
\(\nu = \sqrt{\nu_{i}^{2} + \nu_{Q}^{2} } \quad \text{(26)}\)
The noise magnitudes form concentric rings about the center of Figure 15. The count within each ring provides a distribution of the noise magnitude. The distribution function for the noise envelope is actually a Rayleigh distribution (see Probability, Random Variables, and Stochastic Processes by Papoulis in the References section).
\[ D_{\text{env}}(v) = \frac{v}{\sigma^2} e^{-\frac{v^2}{2\sigma^2}} \quad \text{(27)} \]

Knowing the probability density function, the average of the voltage envelope can be determined using

\[\bar{\nu} = \int_{0} v D_{env}(v)dv = \sigma \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}} \quad \text{(28)} \]

The average power is given by

\[\bar{p} = \int_{0}^{\nu} \frac{v^{2}}{R} D_{env}(v)dv = \frac{2\sigma^{2}}{R} \quad \text{(29)} \]

Calculating the power by squaring the average envelope voltage then dividing by R does not provide the same results as Equation 29. The result is 1.05 dB smaller.
\[\begin{align*}
10\log((\frac{\frac{\nu}{R}}{p}) &= 10\log(\frac{\sigma^{2}\pi R}{4\sigma^{2}R}) \\
&= 10\log(\frac{\pi}{4}) \\
&= -1.05 \text{ dB}
\end{align*}\]

## CONCLUSION

The theory presented in this application note provides a direct relationship between phase noise and jitter and their frequency domain representation. Analysis of phase noise and jitter in the frequency domain highlights the content of the noise signals. Furthermore, measurements in the frequency domain provide enhanced resolution at higher frequencies.
